newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Supreme Court ponders presidential bugging.
newsitem.headline: French Supreme Court ponders presidential bugging.

text.p: A state prosecutor on Tuesday asked France's Supreme Court to reject a bid to stop a probe into alleged widespread illegal phone-tapping by the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand's anti-terrorist unit.

Lawyers for several former senior officials being probed in connection with the scandal, which took place in the mid-1980s, asked the court to declare that the bugging was covered by the statute of limitations and the probe should end.
The Court (Cour de Cassation) said it would deliver its verdict on March 4.

Two former senior government officials, the former head and three members of the since disbanded anti-terrorist unit are being investigated over accusations that the unit tapped the phones of dozens of politicians, lawyers and journalists without the required judicial permission.
The Paris appeals court last September gave investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Vallat the green light to continue the probe into alleged invasion of privacy.
Among those being investigated are Mitterrand's former chief aide Gilles Menage, Prefect Christian Prouteau, who headed the anti-terrorist unit at the Elysee presidential palace.

Louis Schweitzer, the chairman of carmaker Renault, who was at the time chief aide to then prime minister Laurent Fabius, and former labour minister Michel Delebarre, who was chief aide to then prime minister Pierre Mauroy, are also being probed.
